Psalm 22:28: "the kingdom is the Lord's, and he rules over the nations."

Most Christians across traditions read Matthew 25:31-46 as the final judgment at the end of history. Partial preterists who see a transition at 24:36 agree. Dispensationalists place it after the tribulation, when Christ judges the living nations before the millennium.
How should we decide when a prophecy is fulfilled?
Let the time words in the text and its context set the limits. Words like "near," "this generation" and "a long time" mean what they meant to the first hearers.

On this reading, the solution is simple. Look for time indicators in the context and let them set the limits. Everyone admits Matthew 24-25 has time indicators. The question is whether we allow them to govern. Elsewhere, "a long time" (Luke 8:27; Acts 8:11) and "delay" (Luke 1:21; Acts 9:38) have no special end-times meaning. They mean ordinary periods. The returning masters in the parables come back to the same people. The bridegroom arrives the same night. If these words are stretched over two thousand years, the reader is no longer letting the text speak. Good interpretation compares Scripture with Scripture and reads each prophecy from its audience's point of view.
Luke 1:21: the people wondered at Zechariah's "delay" in the temple, a matter of minutes.
Revelation 22:10: "Do not seal up the words... for the time is near," the opposite of Daniel 8:26, where a far vision was sealed.

Other views agree time words matter but add other principles: prophetic foreshortening (near and far events seen together), double fulfillment, and God's different view of time (2 Peter 3:8). They say these allow near words to cover a long church age.
Is a pretribulation rapture the next great event on God's prophetic timetable, on which all prophecy depends?
This reading says no. Scripture never names a pretribulation rapture, so it cannot be the hinge of all prophecy.

Many teachers present the pretribulation rapture as the next event in God's plan and the key that unlocks all other prophecy. On this reading, a doctrine with that much weight should be stated plainly in Scripture. Yet no verse says Christ will come secretly for his church, then return seven years later. The texts often used (John 14:1-3; 1 Thessalonians 4:16-17; 1 Corinthians 15:51-52) speak of Christ's coming and the resurrection. They do not mention a seven-year gap. The New Testament's central future hope is the resurrection of the dead and life with the Lord. A system that hangs everything on an unstated event, this reading argues, has its foundations in the wrong place.
Dave Hunt wrote a chapter titled "The Late Great Rapture Theory," lamenting that many Christians were questioning the doctrine.
Many teachers in the 1970s presented the rapture as the next event that could happen "at any moment."

Pretribulationists answer that the doctrine rests on combining texts: the promise that the church is kept from the hour of trial (Revelation 3:10), not appointed to wrath (1 Thessalonians 5:9), and the absence of the church in Revelation 4-18. They see it as a necessary deduction.
How old is the pretribulation rapture teaching?
It took clear shape around 1830 in the circle of John Nelson Darby and spread through the Scofield Reference Bible (1909).

The idea of a secret coming of Christ for the church, years before his public return, was developed in Britain around 1830. John Nelson Darby, a leader among the Plymouth Brethren, taught and spread it. American Bible conferences and the Scofield Reference Bible (1909) made it common. Even Dave Hunt grants that Darby and Scofield made it dominant for about a hundred years. On this reading, a doctrine unknown to the church fathers, the medieval church and the Reformers needs strong biblical proof. Its newness does not by itself disprove it, but it should make believers cautious about calling it the test of faithful belief.
The Powerscourt prophecy conferences in Ireland (1831-1833) helped spread these ideas.
The Scofield Reference Bible (1909; revised 1917, 1967) carried dispensational notes to millions of readers.

Pretribulationists point to earlier hints, such as a sermon attributed to Pseudo-Ephraem (perhaps 4th-7th century) and the Baptist Morgan Edwards (1788). Others say these sources do not teach the full system. Many also note that age does not decide truth; Scripture does.
Does questioning the rapture mean questioning heaven?
No. The hope of being with Christ at death and in the resurrection is far older and wider than any rapture theory.

Dave Hunt's book Whatever Happened to Heaven? treated the decline in rapture teaching as a decline in hope of heaven. On this reading, that confuses two different things. For eighteen centuries before 1830, the church preached heaven, resurrection and Christ's return without any pretribulation rapture. Paul said that to depart and be with Christ is far better (Philippians 1:21-23). To be away from the body is to be at home with the Lord (2 Corinthians 5:8). Jesus promised the dying thief, "today you will be with me in paradise" (Luke 23:43). No one in this debate denies heaven. The debate is only about the timing and nature of one event.
The Apostles' Creed confesses Christ's return, the resurrection of the body and life everlasting, but says nothing of a rapture before tribulation.
Philippians 1:23: Paul longed to depart and be with Christ.

Pretribulationists answer that the rapture is closely tied to the hope of heaven because it is how living believers are taken there. They say neglect of the rapture often goes with a loss of heavenly-mindedness.
Why did The Late Great Planet Earth capture a whole generation?
It was popular in style, linked current events to prophecy with great confidence, and offered a near timetable.

Hal Lindsey's The Late Great Planet Earth appeared in 1970. It became one of the best-selling non-fiction books of the decade and sold tens of millions of copies in many languages. On this reading, three things explain its success. It was written in an easy, story-like style. It read news events, such as Israel, the Soviet Union and the European Common Market, as fulfilled prophecy with great certainty. And it gave readers a feeling of seeing the future, as its last chapter, "Polishing the Crystal Ball," suggests. Above all, it hinted at a timetable: the generation of 1948 would see the end. A date, even a vague one, draws attention.
Sales of the book jumped sharply during the 1990 Gulf crisis, according to its publisher.
A film version with Orson Welles as narrator was released in 1979.

Supporters say the book brought many people to faith and stirred interest in Scripture. Lindsey himself said he did not set dates, only showed that the signs were present. Critics in all camps faulted its speculation.
How did the "1948 plus 40 years" calculation work, and what happened to it?
Lindsey took a generation as about forty years from 1948, giving 1988 for the end and about 1981 for a pretribulation rapture. Neither happened.

Lindsey read the fig tree as Israel and "this generation" as the one that saw Israel reborn. He suggested a generation was about forty years. Adding forty to 1948 gives 1988. Since he held that the rapture comes seven years before Christ's return to set up his kingdom, the rapture would fall around 1981. On this reading, readers naturally took this as a timetable. Many expected the Lord before 1988. In 1980 Lindsey wrote that the 1980s could very well be the last decade of history as we know it. The decade ended and the forecast failed. Lindsey also wrote that he was not sure how long a biblical generation is, perhaps sixty to eighty years. The calendar kept moving.
Hal Lindsey, The 1980s: Countdown to Armageddon (1980).
In 1975 Baptist scholar Dale Moody wrote that if the rapture happened before the tribulation and by 1981, he would ask Lindsey's pardon when they met in the air.

Lindsey and his defenders say he used cautious words such as "if this is a correct deduction" and "could take place," and never set a fixed date. Many futurists today reject any fixed generation count but still see 1948 as significant.
If Lindsey used cautious words like "if" and "something like forty years," was he really setting dates?
This reading says that in effect he did. He made the calculation and readers acted on it, whatever the hedges.

Lindsey wrote "if this is a correct deduction," "something like forty years" and "could take place." Dave Hunt later said the book only suggested a possible fulfillment within forty years. On this reading, the hedges did not change the effect. Lindsey did the arithmetic. His readers did not treat his words as guesses; many set their hopes on the Lord coming before 1988. When asked in 1977, "What if you're wrong?", Lindsey said there is a split second's difference between a hero and a bum, and if he was wrong he would become a bum. Scripture sets a high bar for those who speak about the future in God's name (Deuteronomy 18:22). Teachers will be judged more strictly (James 3:1).
Christianity Today, April 1977: Lindsey's "hero or bum" reply to W. Ward Gasque.
Lindsey later wrote that a generation might be sixty to eighty years, and that he felt certain the end would come before 2000.

Defenders say it is fair to discuss possibilities and that Lindsey never claimed to be a prophet. They distinguish between suggesting a likely time and setting a date. Even so, most futurist scholars now warn against such counting.
Can "near," "shortly" and "quickly" mean "at any moment" after almost two thousand years?
This reading says no. Those words mean near in time for the first readers. "Any moment" is a different idea.

Tim LaHaye wrote that the Bible teaches Jesus is coming soon, and that he could come for his church at any time. On this reading, "soon" means near in time. Look at how the words are used elsewhere. "Near" in Luke 21:31 and Revelation 1:3. "Shortly" in Acts 25:4, where Festus will leave shortly. "Quickly" in Matthew 28:7-8, where the women run quickly. Try putting "at any moment, perhaps after two thousand years" in those places. It does not work. Revelation says its events "must shortly take place" (Revelation 1:1) and that "the time is near" (Revelation 22:10). This reading holds that a high view of Scripture means taking these words at their plain value.
Acts 25:4: Festus said he would go to Caesarea "shortly," and he went within days (Acts 25:6).
Matthew 28:7-8: "go quickly"; "they departed quickly."

Futurists answer that "quickly" can mean "suddenly" (when it comes, it will come fast), and that "near" means "next in God's plan." Others point to 2 Peter 3:8-9: God's delay is patience, not slowness.
How do Paul's "I hope to send Timothy shortly" and Revelation's "must shortly take place" compare?
Paul added "I hope" because his plan might change. Revelation adds no such qualifier; God says these things "must" happen soon.

Paul writes, "I hope in the Lord Jesus to send Timothy to you shortly" (Philippians 2:19). He also trusts he himself will come shortly (Philippians 2:24). John writes, "I hope to see you shortly" (3 John 14). In each case "shortly" means soon, but the writer adds a qualifier because human plans can change. On this reading, Revelation 1:1 is different. God gave the revelation to show his servants things that "must shortly take place." There is no "I hope," only "must." Revelation 22:6 repeats it. If even a human "shortly" means soon, a divine "must shortly" cannot mean thousands of years later.
Philippians 2:23: Paul will send Timothy "as soon as I see how it will go with me."
Revelation 22:6: "the things which must shortly be done."

Futurists say "shortly" (en tachei) in Revelation can mean "quickly" in manner, so when the events begin they will move fast. Historicists see Revelation's events beginning soon after John wrote and continuing through history.
Is anyone who denies a pretribulation rapture reading the Bible "as allegory"?
This reading says no. It takes time words literally, which is the opposite of allegory.

Tim LaHaye wrote that those who reject a pretribulation rapture interpret the Bible figuratively or as allegory. On this reading, that charge is unfair. The fulfilled reading takes Jesus' time words, "this generation," "near," "shortly," plainly. It reads Old Testament symbolic language the way the prophets used it. That is not allegory. It is reading Scripture by its own patterns. It is also striking that LaHaye admitted no single passage teaches two aspects of Christ's coming separated by the tribulation. A doctrine admitted to have no single clear text should not be used to call others unbiblical. Both sides want a Bible that is inspired and without error.
LaHaye, No Fear of the Storm (1992): no one passage teaches the two stages, but no passage teaches a post- or mid-trib rapture either.
Galatians 4:24 shows Paul himself using an allegory openly, which is different from symbolic prophecy.

Pretribulationists answer that their method is consistent literal reading of prophecy, especially of Israel's promises, and that reading "Israel" as the church or cosmic signs as symbols is a step toward allegory.
Is there a single Bible verse that clearly teaches a pretribulation rapture?
Leading supporters admit there is none. They build the doctrine from inferences rather than one explicit text.

Tim LaHaye admitted that no one passage teaches two stages of the coming separated by the tribulation. Marvin Rosenthal, once a pretribulationist, observed that John Walvoord's The Rapture Question offered fifty arguments but no text that explicitly teaches the view. Walvoord himself said the rapture question is settled more by ecclesiology (the doctrine of the church) than by eschatology (the doctrine of the last things). On this reading, this is a remarkable admission. Millions hold the doctrine with deep conviction, yet its leading defenders concede it rests on deduction. This reading adds that no future-rapture timing view, pre, mid or post, has a clear verse, because the texts used are mostly about AD 70 or the final resurrection.
Rosenthal, The Pre-Wrath Rapture of the Church (1990), explained why he left the pretribulation view.
Walvoord, The Rapture Question (1957, revised 1979), listed fifty arguments for the position.

Pretribulationists answer that many accepted doctrines, such as the Trinity, are drawn from several texts rather than one. They see the pretribulation rapture as the best way to harmonize texts on imminence, wrath and the church.
Why did the 1990-1991 Gulf crisis set off a new wave of rapture fever?
Teachers read Iraq as Babylon restored and the crisis as the road to Armageddon. The rapture did not come, and the predictions faded.

Iraq invaded Kuwait in August 1990. Prophecy books appeared quickly. One writer presented Saddam Hussein's Iraq as the rise of Babylon in the end times. John Walvoord's Armageddon, Oil and the Middle East Crisis was revised and sold widely. Asked if the end of history was beginning in the Gulf, Hal Lindsey said prophecy was "on fast forward" and that he believed this was the generation that would see Armageddon. On this reading, this was one more round of reading the newspaper into the Bible. The war ended in February 1991. No Antichrist rose, no rapture came, and many readers were left confused.
Charles Dyer, The Rise of Babylon: Sign of the End Times (1991).
Lindsey's 1970 book saw sales jump sharply between August and September 1990.
Futurists answer that a literal rebuilt Babylon (Revelation 17-18) is still expected, and that watching world events in light of prophecy is a duty (Matthew 16:3), even if particular forecasts fail.
What is "newspaper exegesis," and why is it dangerous?
It means reading the Bible through current events. History shows that every generation using it has been wrong.

The phrase, used by Greg Bahnsen, describes interpreting Scripture by today's headlines. On this reading, the newspaper has no right to set the meaning of God's word. Teachers claim to read the news in light of the Bible, but in practice the news shapes the reading. History is full of examples. When Germanic tribes overran Rome in the fifth century, many Christians thought the world was ending. Many expected the end around the year 1000. In the troubled fourteenth century, tracts announced the last age of the church. All used the same verses now used today. The historian Iain Murray made this point in The Puritan Hope (1971). Confidence each time was high, and each time it was wrong.
Rome was sacked by the Visigoths in AD 410. Augustine wrote The City of God partly to answer the panic.
Many in the 1500s identified the Turkish advance with Gog or the beast.

Futurists answer that Jesus rebuked people who could read the sky but not "the signs of the times" (Matthew 16:3), so Christians should watch world events. Most agree that dogmatic identifications are unwise.
Is the rapture or the resurrection the true hope of the church?
The resurrection. Paul stood trial for the resurrection of the dead, and the whole gospel hangs on Christ's resurrection and ours.

Paul said he was on trial "concerning the resurrection of the dead" (Acts 24:21). He argued that if there is no resurrection, Christ has not been raised, and preaching and faith are empty (1 Corinthians 15:13-14). His goal was to attain to the resurrection from the dead (Philippians 3:11). On this reading, the New Testament never makes such a defense of a pre-, mid- or post-tribulation rapture. The heart of Christian hope is that Christ is risen and that those who are his will be raised. The rapture debate, this reading argues, has turned eyes from that centre. Without the resurrection the Christian message is one religious idea among many. With it, believers have a sure hope.
1 Corinthians 15:20: Christ is the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep.
Acts 4:2: the apostles were arrested for preaching "in Jesus the resurrection from the dead."

Pretribulationists agree the resurrection is central and say the rapture is part of it: the dead in Christ rise first (1 Thessalonians 4:16). They see the "blessed hope" (Titus 2:13) as Christ's appearing for his church, which includes the resurrection.
How can Christians avoid "rapture fever" and still live with hope?
Read prophecy in its setting, refuse date-setting, keep the resurrection central, and work faithfully under Christ's present reign.

On this reading, rapture fever grows when people tear prophecies from their audience, ignore time words, and read headlines into Scripture. The cure is to read each text as its first hearers would. Refuse every form of date-setting, even soft forms (Acts 1:7). Keep the gospel's centre in view: Christ crucified, risen and reigning (1 Corinthians 15:3-4, 25). Live as faithful servants who are found working when the master comes (Matthew 24:45-46). Plan, build and serve for the long term, as Jeremiah told exiles to build houses and plant gardens (Jeremiah 29:5-7). Hope rests on Christ's promises, not on the news.
Some believers who expected the rapture by 1981 or 1988 put off long-term plans, such as study or saving, and later had to rethink.
1 Thessalonians 4:11-12 tells believers to live quietly, mind their own affairs and work with their hands, right after Paul's teaching on the Lord's coming.

All views agree date-setting is wrong. Futurists add that hope of Christ's soon return should motivate holy living (1 John 3:2-3) and urgent evangelism, and that this hope is healthy when kept free of speculation.
Is there a single verse that plainly teaches a rapture before a future tribulation?
On the fulfilled reading, no. Each text offered for it speaks of Christ's coming or the resurrection, but none says the church leaves seven years before a final tribulation.

Read on its own terms, no verse states that the church will be removed from the earth before a seven-year tribulation. The texts most often used, such as 1 Thessalonians 4:16-17, 1 Corinthians 15:51-52 and Revelation 4:1, speak of resurrection, change and meeting the Lord. They do not mention a tribulation period or a second, later coming. Even some writers who hold the view admit that no verse proves its timing and that it is built by deduction from a wider system. This system depends on placing a gap between Daniel's sixty-ninth and seventieth weeks (Daniel 9:24-27). The fulfilled reading asks for a clear text before a doctrine becomes a pillar of belief. The Bereans tested teaching against Scripture (Acts 17:11), and this reading asks for the same test here.

A test case: read 1 Thessalonians 4:13-18 aloud and list every event named. You will find the descent of the Lord, a shout, a trumpet, the resurrection and the meeting. You will not find a tribulation, seven years, or a return to heaven.
In 1989 a leading pre-tribulation writer said that neither pre- nor post-tribulation believers have a proof text for timing, and that the issue is a deduction from one's system.

Pre-tribulation teachers answer that the doctrine rests on several lines that combine: the promise of being kept from the hour of trial (Revelation 3:10), deliverance from wrath (1 Thessalonians 1:10; 5:9), imminence, and the distinction between Israel and the church. They argue that the Trinity is also taught by combining texts rather than by one verse.
Is "Come up here" in Revelation 4:1 a picture of the rapture of the church?
Read in context, no. John alone is called up in a vision to see what follows; the voice is only "like" a trumpet, and John stays in his body on Patmos.

In Revelation 4:1 John sees an open door in heaven and hears a voice "as it were of a trumpet" call him up. The words are spoken to John, not to the church. Even a strong pre-tribulation scholar, John Walvoord, granted that the verse is not an explicit reference to the rapture, since John stayed in his natural body on Patmos. He only saw it as a "type". The fulfilled reading notes three points. First, John hears a voice like a trumpet, not a trumpet. Second, prophets are often taken up "in the Spirit" to see visions (Ezekiel 3:12-14; 8:3), and no one calls those raptures. Third, the call is to "show" John what must happen soon (Revelation 1:1). It is a call to see, not a removal of the church.
Ezekiel was lifted "between earth and heaven" by the Spirit and brought to Jerusalem in visions (Ezekiel 8:3). He was not raptured; he saw a vision.
Paul was "caught up" to the third heaven (2 Corinthians 12:2-4), but no one reads that as the church's departure.

Some pre-tribulation writers see a typical pattern here: the letters to the churches (chapters 2-3), then a summons to heaven, then judgments on earth (chapters 6-19). Most careful pre-tribulation scholars use the verse only as an illustration of the order of events, not as proof.
Does the word "church" disappearing after Revelation 3 prove the church has been removed?
On the fulfilled reading, no. Word counts cannot decide doctrine. Many New Testament books never use the word "church", and Revelation 22:16 says the whole book is for the churches.

Chapters 2-3 address seven local congregations by name, so the word "churches" appears often there. After chapter 3 John speaks of "saints" and "servants", the people who make up those churches (Revelation 13:7, 10; 14:12; 19:8). The argument from silence fails when tested elsewhere. The word "church" is absent from Mark, Luke, John, 2 Timothy, Titus, 1 Peter, 2 Peter, 1 John, 2 John and Jude, yet no one says these books are not for the church. The word "Israel" also appears only once in Revelation 4-19 (7:4), though that section is said to be about Israel. The word "antichrist" never appears in Revelation at all, yet many find him there. Finally, Jesus says the whole testimony is "for the churches" (Revelation 22:16).
Esther never names God, yet God is clearly at work in the story. Silence about a word is not absence of the thing.
Revelation 22:16: "I, Jesus, have sent my angel to testify these things to you for the assemblies" (WEB), placed at the end of the book.

Pre-tribulation writers reply that the change of vocabulary is still significant: the formal church language and the call "hear what the Spirit says to the churches" stop after chapter 3. In 13:9 the call becomes "If anyone has an ear", which they see as addressing tribulation saints rather than the church.
Are the "saints" in Revelation 4-19 a different group from the church?
Read with the rest of the New Testament, no. "Saints" is a normal name for church members, so the saints in Revelation are the church under trial.

Paul writes "to the church of God which is at Corinth ... called to be saints" (1 Corinthians 1:2). The church and the saints are the same people seen from two sides: the assembly as a body, and its members as holy ones. Paul uses this pattern often (Romans 1:7; Ephesians 1:1; Philippians 1:1). In Revelation the saints offer prayers (5:8; 8:3-4), suffer persecution (13:7, 10), keep the commands of God and the faith of Jesus (14:12), and are clothed in righteous acts (19:8). "The faith of Jesus" is a Christian mark, not a sign of a separate Israel-only group. On the fulfilled reading, the saints of chapters 4-19 are the believers of the seven churches and their brothers facing the trial John said was near.
1 Corinthians 1:2 places "church" and "saints" in the same sentence for the same people.
Revelation 14:12 describes the saints as those who keep "the faith of Jesus", which is the confession of the church.

Dispensational writers hold that the saints of the tribulation are people who come to faith after the rapture, including converted Jews and Gentiles. They are true believers, but they are not part of the church age body.
Do the seven churches of Revelation 2-3 stand for seven ages of church history?
On this reading, no. The seven were real congregations in Asia Minor, and nothing in the text says they map onto later eras.

John writes to seven churches in real cities on a postal road in western Asia Minor (Revelation 1:11). Each letter speaks to local facts: Laodicea's lukewarm water and wealth, Smyrna's coming ten-day trial, Pergamum's "throne of Satan". Some writers say the letters picture seven ages, for example Smyrna for the persecutions of the second to fourth centuries, and Sardis for the Reformation. The text gives no such key. The scheme also forces odd results: Sardis, a church that was "dead" (3:1), becomes the Reformation. The Reformed scholar William Hendriksen judged that there is no evidence in Scripture for this division of church history. The letters, like the rest of the book, concern things that would "shortly come to pass" for those readers (1:1).
Laodicea had no good water supply of its own. Water came by aqueduct and arrived lukewarm. This gives local colour to Revelation 3:15-16.
Smyrna is told of a trial of "ten days" (2:10), a short, local test, not a three-century era.

Historicist and many dispensational writers (for example C. I. Scofield) see the seven letters as both local and prophetic of church history, with Laodicea as the lukewarm last age. Others in those traditions hold only that the letters give lasting types of churches found in every age.
Can Christ's coming be "at any moment" if the seven church ages must run first?
On the fulfilled reading, the two ideas clash. If six ages had to pass before Laodicea, the early church could not expect Christ at any moment.

Many pre-tribulation teachers hold two beliefs together. First, the rapture is imminent: it could happen at any moment, and first-century believers expected it in their lifetime. Second, the seven churches of Revelation 2-3 picture seven successive ages, with the last age, Laodicea, just before the rapture. These cannot both be true for the first readers. If Smyrna stands for the second to fourth centuries and Sardis for the Reformation, then Christ could not come until those ages had passed. This reading also leaves the literal method, because the seven churches are no longer treated as seven real churches. The fulfilled reading resolves the tension differently: Christ said he would come "quickly" to those churches (2:16; 3:11), and that coming was near for them.
A worked comparison: if Christ could return in AD 95, the Reformation "age" of Sardis would never have come. If Sardis had to come, Christ could not return in AD 95.
Revelation 3:11 tells Philadelphia, "I come quickly. Hold firmly what you have" (WEB).

Some dispensationalists answer that the church-age pattern is visible only in hindsight. In this view, God veiled the sequence so each generation could still expect Christ. Others drop the seven-ages view and keep imminence.
Is the rider on the white horse in Revelation 19 a picture of Christ's bodily second coming?
Read symbolically, it is a picture of Christ's judging victory, not the bodily return. Acts 1:11 says he will come as he went: with a cloud, not on a horse.

Dispensational teaching sees two stages: Christ comes for his saints before the tribulation, then with his saints in Revelation 19. Yet the church is not named in Revelation 19. The "armies in heaven" follow him (19:14). If these armies are the church, then the church can be present without the word, which undoes the argument from silence in Revelation 4-19. Robert Thomas calls Revelation 19 the one passage in the book that matches the personal coming of Christ. The fulfilled reading notes that Acts 1:9-11 says Jesus will come "in the same way" he went: received by a cloud, not riding a horse. The white horse belongs to symbolic war imagery. Christ's weapon is the sword from his mouth (19:15), which is his word.
Acts 1:9: "a cloud received him out of their sight" (WEB). No horse is involved.
Christ strikes the nations with "a sharp, double-edged sword" from his mouth (Revelation 19:15). This is plainly symbolic, like Hebrews 4:12.

Most futurists, and many amillennial and postmillennial readers too, take Revelation 19:11-21 as a symbolic picture of the real, bodily second coming at the end of history. They argue that symbols can depict a literal event, as the cloud in Acts 1 also points to his return.
